title: A curve from a P10 remaining life

blocks.text: A district-heating company's analytics team predicts, for every pump, the number of years `r` by which there is a chance `q` that a pump working today at age `age` will have failed. Most reports use `q = 0.1`, the P10 remaining life, because the crews plan to it; a few use the median, `q = 0.5`. The reliability team supplies one shape `beta` per pump type. The risk model needs a whole curve per pump.

Write `scale_from_report(age, r, q, beta)` in `calibrate.py`: the scale `eta` (years) of the Weibull curve with shape `beta` on which a pump working at `age` has exactly the chance `q` of failing within the next `r` years.

The lesson solved this for the median. Write the condition for a general `q` in its notation, $`R(a + r)/R(a) = 1 - q`$, and solve it for $`\eta`$ before you code. The tests check the curve you return with `scipy.stats.weibull_min`. One or two lines.

import math


def scale_from_report(age: float, r: float, q: float, beta: float) -> float:
    """The scale on which a unit working at `age` fails within `r` years with chance `q`."""
    # TODO: solve R(age + r) / R(age) = 1 - q for eta.
    return r


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(scale_from_report(25, 6, 0.1, 3.5))

cases.says: for a new unit reported at the median, the curve's median lifetime is the reported years
a report at the 10% level makes the chance of failing within the reported years 10%
for a unit in service, the chance is that of failing within the reported years given it works today
